meta.title: The Solar Odyssey timeline
meta.description: Milestones in the history of solar power and the wider renewable-energy system, grouped into four eras of a day: dawn (discovery), morning (understanding and the first real cells), midday (the industry and the cost collapse) and afternoon (today's research frontier). 'track' is 'solar' or 'renewables'; 'status' marks settled history, current consensus or active research; 'checks' tie numbers in the text to other datasets and are re-verified by tests/unit/timeline.test.mjs.
meta.units: years (CE); numbers in the text carry their own units

data.title: A glimmer of current
data.text: In Paris, 19-year-old Edmond Becquerel dipped two metal electrodes, one of them coated, into a conducting liquid and shone light on one of them. The current between them changed when the light came on. It was the first recorded photovoltaic effect: light making electricity directly, with nothing moving.
data.expert: Becquerel reported the effect to the Académie des sciences in 1839. His cell was electrochemical, not solid-state, and nobody could yet explain it: the electron would not be discovered for another 58 years.

data.title: Selenium feels the light
data.text: Willoughby Smith, an engineer testing undersea telegraph cables, used bars of selenium as high-value resistors. He found their resistance dropped sharply when light fell on them. Light was changing how well a solid conducts electricity.
data.expert: This is photoconductivity, not the photovoltaic effect: the selenium still needed a battery to drive the current. Light only freed extra charge carriers.

data.title: Electricity from a solid, with no battery
data.text: William Grylls Adams and Richard Evans Day pressed heated platinum contacts into a piece of selenium and shone light on it. A current flowed with no battery in the circuit at all. It was the first photovoltaic effect in a solid, the ancestor of every solar panel.
data.expert: Adams and Day guessed wrongly that light was crystallising the outer layer of the selenium. The real explanation needed the quantum theory of solids, half a century later.

data.title: Falling water lights a town
data.text: On the Fox River in Appleton, Wisconsin, a waterwheel turned an Edison dynamo in the Vulcan Street Plant. It first lit two paper mills and a house, and within weeks more homes and a hotel. It was the first Edison hydroelectric central station in North America to serve paying customers.

data.title: The first flat solar cell
data.text: Charles Fritts spread a thin layer of selenium on a metal plate and covered it with gold leaf so thin that light passed through. His cells reached about 30 square centimetres. They turned only a tiny fraction of sunlight into electricity, but the layout, a thin light-catching layer between two contacts, is the one panels still use.

data.title: Ultraviolet light helps a spark
data.text: While proving that radio waves exist, Heinrich Hertz noticed that a spark jumped a gap more easily when ultraviolet light fell on the metal. Light was pulling charge out of the metal surface. This photoelectric effect became a puzzle that classical physics could not solve.

data.title: A windmill that charged batteries
data.text: Behind his house in Cleveland, Charles Brush built a wind turbine with a rotor about 17 metres across and 144 slender blades. It turned a dynamo that charged storage batteries, which lit the house. It is one of the first wind turbines built to make electricity.

data.title: Storing the wind as hydrogen
data.text: At Askov in Denmark, Poul la Cour tested an electricity-making windmill and used its current to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. From 1895 the gas lit the local school, even on days when the wind was still. It was an early answer to the question every renewable grid still asks: how do you keep energy for later?

data.title: Earth heat lights five bulbs
data.text: At Larderello in Tuscany, Prince Piero Ginori Conti used natural steam from the ground to drive a small generator and lit five light bulbs. In 1913 the first commercial geothermal plant opened on the same site with a 250-kilowatt turbine. Larderello still makes geothermal power today.

data.title: Light comes in packets
data.text: Albert Einstein proposed that light travels as packets of energy, later called photons, and that each packet's energy depends only on its colour. That explained why dim ultraviolet light frees electrons while bright red light does not. The same idea tells us which colours of sunlight a solar cell can use.
data.expert: Einstein predicted that the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron is E = hf − W, where W is the work function of the metal. He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics (awarded in 1922) especially for this law of the photoelectric effect.

data.title: A doubter confirms the photon
data.text: Robert Millikan set out to test Einstein's formula with careful measurements. They matched it, and gave a value for Planck's constant, the number that links a photon's colour to its energy.
data.expert: Millikan plotted the stopping voltage against light frequency for several metals and found straight lines with the same slope, h/e, exactly as E = hf − W predicts.

data.title: Pulling a perfect crystal
data.text: Jan Czochralski, studying how fast metals crystallise, pulled a thin thread of metal slowly up out of a molten bath. It came out as a single crystal. Decades later the same method became the standard way to grow the large, flawless silicon crystals that most solar cells are cut from.

data.title: The crack that made a junction
data.text: At Bell Labs, Russell Ohl was testing a rod of purified silicon. When light shone on it, the rod produced a voltage by itself. Two parts of the crystal held different impurities, and the boundary between them, a p-n junction, pushed the light-freed charges apart.
data.expert: Ohl's patent (filed 1941, granted 1946 as US 2,402,662) describes a light-sensitive barrier that forms by itself as purified silicon cools and solidifies slowly, because impurities collect unevenly. He also listed solar power among its uses.

data.title: The first practical solar cell
data.text: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson at Bell Labs built a silicon cell that turned about 6 percent of sunlight into electricity, more than ten times better than selenium. For the first time, sunlight was a usable power source.
data.expert: They formed the p-n junction by diffusing an impurity a very short way into the surface of the silicon, so the junction sat close to where most light is absorbed. The I-V curve lesson shows how efficiency follows from the current and voltage such a cell delivers.

data.title: A satellite that runs on sunlight
data.text: Vanguard 1 was the first satellite powered by the Sun. Six small solar cells on its body ran a radio transmitter for more than six years, long after its battery-powered transmitter had gone silent. Space was solar's first real market: in orbit, cost mattered less than weight and reliability.
data.expert: Vanguard 1 is still in orbit, the oldest human-made object there. Space missions pushed the development of radiation-hardened and later multi-junction cells.

data.title: The ceiling for a single cell
data.text: William Shockley and Hans-Joachim Queisser worked out the best efficiency any cell made of one material could ever reach. Photons with too little energy pass straight through, and the extra energy of the rest is lost as heat. For a material like silicon they found a ceiling of about 30 percent.
data.expert: Their detailed-balance argument says a cell that absorbs light must also emit it, so radiative recombination sets an unavoidable loss. Their 30 % figure assumed a 1.1 eV band gap and the Sun as a 6000 K black body; recalculations with today's standard spectrum give a somewhat higher peak, for band gaps near 1.3–1.4 eV.

data.title: A dam that runs on the tide
data.text: The Rance tidal power station in Brittany, France, was inaugurated with 24 turbines and 240 megawatts of capacity. The tide fills and empties the estuary behind a barrage, and the moving water turns the turbines. It was the world's first tidal power station and it still runs.

data.title: The oil shock
data.text: During the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, Arab oil producers cut supplies to the United States and its allies, and the price of oil first doubled and then quadrupled. Governments suddenly wanted energy they did not have to import. Money began to flow into solar power on the ground, not just in space.

data.title: A very expensive watt
data.text: In 1975 a solar module cost about $132 per watt of capacity, in today's money. At that price, panels for a typical home roof would have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. Almost the only buyers were satellites and remote equipment.

data.title: Thin-film silicon
data.text: David Carlson and Christopher Wronski at RCA Laboratories made a solar cell from amorphous silicon, a disordered form that can be deposited as a very thin film. It used far less material than a slice of crystal. It opened the thin-film branch of solar technology.

data.title: A national solar laboratory
data.text: The United States opened the Solar Energy Research Institute in Golden, Colorado, as a direct response to the oil crisis. In 1991 it became the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), whose chart of record cell efficiencies is the reference the field still uses. In December 2025 it was renamed the National Laboratory of the Rockies.

data.title: The first megawatt
data.text: ARCO Solar opened a 1.1-megawatt solar power plant at Hesperia, California, the first plant of that size in the United States. The next year it built a 5.2-megawatt plant on the Carrizo Plain. Solar had moved from rooftops and satellites to power stations.

data.title: A cell that wastes less
data.text: At the University of New South Wales, Andrew Blakers, Martin Green and colleagues reported a silicon cell with 22.8 percent efficiency. Its trick was to treat the back surface so that fewer freed electrons were lost there. Factories adopted the design decades later, and it made mass-produced panels much better.
data.expert: The design is PERC, the passivated emitter and rear cell: a dielectric layer passivates most of the rear surface, with local openings for the metal contact, cutting rear-surface recombination.

data.title: Wind turbines go to sea
data.text: Eleven 450-kilowatt turbines were set in shallow water 1.5 to 3 kilometres off Vindeby, Denmark, making the world's first offshore wind farm, about 5 megawatts in all. Winds at sea are stronger and steadier than on land. Over 25 years it produced 243 gigawatt-hours before it was taken down in 2017.

data.title: A cell made like a leaf
data.text: Brian O'Regan and Michael Grätzel built a cell in which a dye soaks up light, as chlorophyll does, and hands its electrons to a sponge of tiny titanium dioxide particles. It reached about 7 percent efficiency using cheap materials. Its layout later became the starting point for perovskite cells.

data.title: Germany guarantees the price
data.text: Germany's Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) gave anyone who fed solar, wind or other renewable electricity into the grid a fixed price for 20 years, and priority access to the grid. Renewables then supplied about 6 percent of Germany's electricity. The guaranteed market pulled factories, installers and banks into solar.
data.expert: A feed-in tariff sets a technology-specific price per kilowatt-hour; the first EEG offered up to about 50 euro cents per kWh for solar. Similar laws spread to many countries, and the rising demand drove manufacturing scale and learning.

data.title: Perovskites enter
data.text: Akihiro Kojima, Tsutomu Miyasaka and colleagues in Japan used a lead-halide perovskite, a crystal that can be made from solution at low temperature, as the light absorber in a dye-type cell. It converted 3.8 percent of sunlight. Few noticed at first.
data.expert: The absorber was methylammonium lead iodide (CH3NH3PbI3) on titanium dioxide, with a liquid electrolyte that quickly degraded it.

data.title: Perovskites turn solid
data.text: Teams led by Nam-Gyu Park and Michael Grätzel replaced the liquid with a solid layer and reported perovskite cells above 9 percent efficiency that kept working for weeks. Research groups around the world switched to perovskites. Within a decade their efficiency rivalled silicon's.
data.expert: Replacing the liquid electrolyte with a solid hole-transporting layer stopped the perovskite from dissolving, which had made the 2009 cells degrade quickly.

data.title: A battery the size of a power station
data.text: In South Australia, a 100-megawatt, 129-megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery was completed in November 2017, then the largest of its kind. It showed that batteries could do more than store energy: they could help keep the grid stable. It was expanded to 150 megawatts in 2020.

data.title: Manufacturing at vast scale
data.text: China's industrial policy built solar factories on a scale nobody else matched. By 2022 the International Energy Agency counted China's share of every key manufacturing step, from purified silicon to finished panels, at over 80 percent. That scale helped make solar the cheapest new electricity in much of the world, and it concentrated the supply chain in one country.

data.title: One terawatt
data.text: By the end of 2022 the world had about 1.2 terawatts of solar panels installed, passing the terawatt mark. In 2022 alone the world added about 240 gigawatts.

data.title: About 27 cents a watt
data.text: By 2024 a solar module cost about 27 cents per watt in the same constant dollars, down from $132 in 1975: roughly 500 times cheaper. Few manufactured products have ever fallen in price this far. The cost now lies as much in land, labour, wiring and finance as in the panels.
data.expert: From $132.4 to $0.265 per watt over 49 years is an average fall of about 12 % a year. Prices plotted against cumulative production fall along a nearly straight line on log axes, the 'learning curve' explored in the cost lesson.

data.title: Solar makes 8.7 percent of the world's electricity
data.text: In 2025 solar panels generated about 8.7 percent of the world's electricity, up from less than 0.01 percent in 2000. Nearly 3 terawatts were installed by the end of the year, about 700 gigawatts of it added in 2025 alone, by the count of the IEA's PV programme; IRENA's count of grid-connected capacity, used elsewhere on this site, is lower, about 2.4 terawatts. The question has shifted from cost to fitting so much daytime power into the grid.

data.title: Silicon nears its limit
data.text: A silicon cell with all its contacts on the back, made by LONGi, was certified at 28.29 percent efficiency, up from 27.81 percent in 2025. The practical limit for a silicon cell is about 29.4 percent, so there is little room left. That is why researchers now stack other materials on top of silicon.
data.expert: The 29.4 % limit (Richter, Hermle and Glunz, 2013) includes Auger recombination, which the Shockley-Queisser model ignores, for an ideal 110 µm undoped silicon wafer under the standard spectrum.

data.title: Two layers beat one
data.text: A perovskite layer stacked on a silicon cell reached 35.5 percent efficiency, certified by the European Commission's test laboratory (ESTI). That is well above what any single-material cell can reach. Each layer catches the colours it uses best, so less energy is lost as heat.
data.expert: The perovskite top cell has a wider band gap and absorbs blue and green light; silicon underneath takes the red and near-infrared. The record cell's area was not disclosed; the same company reported 34.3 % on a 261 cm² cell.

data.title: The open question: will it last?
data.text: Silicon panels are expected to work for 25 years or more. Perovskites are still being proven over such long times: heat, moisture and light can slowly break them down. Researchers now test them under agreed procedures so that results from different labs can be compared.
